Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.

title: Multi-Agent Coordination Through Stigmergy for Canal Network Formation on Real Terrain
summary: Terrain-modifying robot swarms operating in unstructured outdoor environments must coordinate under uncertain dynamics despite unreliable communication and incomplete global information. Stigmergy offers a decentralized alternative by allowing agents to coordinate indirectly through persistent environmental modifications, yet its application to large-scale terrain construction on real landscapes remains largely unexplored. Inspired by beaver canal construction, we present a minimal stigmergic framework for multi-agent systems in which decentralized agents follow local wetness cues, excavate terrain, and interact through a closed agent--environmental feedback loop. The framework couples agents with seasonal hydrology on a real digital elevation model (DEM). Across 110 simulations on an 862m x 1167m region spanning agent count and hydrological recession rate, the model produces emergent canal-like networks whose morphology varies predictably with environmental constraints. An alignment-invariant morphological evaluation against a field-annotated reference network identifies parameter regimes that reproduce key canal characteristics, while failure cases reveal over-canalization and fragmentation. These results demonstrate that simple local terrain-modifying behaviors can generate plausible landscape-scale structures through environmental feedback, providing a minimal framework for studying decentralized terrain construction and bio-inspired swarm coordination.

title: From Historical Schedules to On-Sky Control: Autonomous Scheduling on the 4-m Blanco Telescope
summary: The scientific efficiency of ground-based astronomical observatories relies on effective decision-making in a dynamic, multi-timescale environment with complex scientific rewards. Traditional observation schedulers are designed and tuned by domain experts to handle these considerations using heuristic rules based on models of the environment and observational system. Here, we leverage historical data to train an automated telescope scheduler using behavior cloning (BC). The BC scheduler is trained purely on historical datasets; it is not given expert scheduling heuristics nor an optimal scientific reward. It is then evaluated in order of increasing realism: first on expert states, then in closed-loop offline rollouts, and finally during autonomous operation with real-time feedback on the NSF's Victor M.\ Blanco 4-m Telescope. On expert states from holdout nights, the BC policy closely matches the expert distribution over airmass and Moon separation. During closed-loop rollouts on the same nights, we find that the per-observation data-quality metric, $t_{\rm eff}$, falls by $6.9 \pm 3.4\%$ relative to the expert's. During on-sky deployment, the policy scheduled $149$ exposures in $5.2$ hours with an average $t_{\rm eff} = 0.75 \pm 0.26$, consistent with closed-loop rollout evaluations. No additional degradation was observed when transitioning to real observing conditions. This represents the first real-world, real-time deployment of a learned autonomous scheduler on a leadership-class national observatory and establishes a path toward on-sky evaluation of reinforcement-learning-based schedulers trained on archival schedules augmented with counterfactual trajectories.

title: Anomalous front propagation in many-body quantum transport with memory-dependent resetting
summary: We introduce an exactly solvable framework for non-Markovian quantum many-body dynamics based on stochastic resetting with memory. Applicable to arbitrary time-independent Hamiltonians, including interacting systems, our framework provides an exact representation of the dynamics with memory in terms of the corresponding reset-free evolution, which can be accessed either analytically or numerically. We demonstrate the power of this approach by studying domain-wall melting in a one-dimensional chain of noninteracting fermions, obtaining exact analytical results for the density profile, the local structure of the front edge, the extreme-value statistics of the rightmost fermion, and the integrated current. Remarkably, memory transforms ballistic transport into logarithmically slow propagation without arresting spreading. While the macroscopic density profile retains its original scaling function, the front edge broadens as $\sqrt{\ln t}$ rather than $t^{1/3}$ at late times and develops a qualitatively different edge structure. Furthermore, the extreme-value statistics change from Tracy--Widom to Gaussian, while both the mean and variance of the integrated current grow logarithmically in time. Our predictions are in excellent agreement with numerical simulations. These results reveal how memory can fundamentally alter quantum many-body transport and its fluctuations.

title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
summary: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
summary: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.

title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains
summary: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.

title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
summary: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.

title: FedTumor-IoMT: Federated Learning-Aided Brain Tumor Diagnosis on Resource-Constrained Edge IoMT Devices
summary: Joint brain tumor segmentation and classification models are computationally intensive, limiting their training on resource-constrained edge platforms and restricting privacy-preserving Federated Learning FL in the Internet of Medical Things IoMT. Existing approaches either perform both tasks on GPU-equipped workstations or support only classification on edge devices. To address this gap, this work proposes a lightweight multitask FL framework for joint segmentation and classification through local edge training. A shared pretrained LiteMedSAM encoder with TinyViT extracts features for a coordinate-attention-based segmentation decoder and a segmentation-guided classification head, eliminating a separate feature extractor. Selective encoder freezing retains 95\% trainable parameters while reducing on-device training costs. The proposed framework is experimentally validated on a laboratory testbed of five resource-constrained edge clients using 1,200 T1-weighted MRI samples. It achieves 94.20\% classification accuracy, 88.53\% DSC, 83.68\% IoU, and 99.87\% ROC-AUC. Its classification accuracy remains within 0.6\% of the GPU-trained baseline of 95.21\% across five FL rounds. The attention and feature refinement modules improve DSC and IoU by 3.82\% and 4.60\%, respectively, with 0.74 GFLOPs of additional computation. On edge hardware, the framework achieves 46.54 s inference latency, 52.8\% CPU utilization, and a peak temperature of 65$^\circ$C without thermal throttling. Its inference latency is observed to be 6.4--10.5 times lower than that of existing frameworks. These results demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving joint brain tumor segmentation and classification on resource-constrained edge platforms.

title: Beyond Expected Value: PPO with Distributional Critics for Systematic Conservation Planning
summary: Systematic conservation planning must allocate limited protection budgets sequentially under ecological and climatic uncertainty. Static tools cannot adapt as conditions change, and policies optimised only for expected outcomes can fail on the worst-case trajectories climate change makes increasingly likely. CAPTAIN was the first framework to cast this as sequential reinforcement learning, but its gradient-free Evolution Strategies (ES) optimiser lacks per-timestep credit assignment. We replace ES with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) via a Plackett-Luce solution to CAPTAIN's non-differentiable action space, and replace its scalar critic with an Implicit Quantile Network (IQN) modelling the full return distribution. A matched-granularity comparison shows decision granularity, not the optimiser, drives most of the ecological gain, so the real contribution is training efficiency and extensibility to risk-sensitive objectives. On a New Zealand marine dataset, it matches or exceeds ES's outcomes at a fraction of the training cost, offering a template for future work ES's black-box design could not support

title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
summary: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.

title: DynaMimic: A Physics-Informed World Model for Humanoid Motion Tracking
summary: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.

title: Fast and Accurate Boys Function Evaluation Using Nonuniform Gridded Taylor Expansions
summary: Efficient Boys function evaluation is important for Gaussian integral calculations on both central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs). Gridded Taylor expansion provides a simple evaluation procedure, but a uniformly spaced reference table requires substantial storage over a wide argument range. We address this limitation using a nonuniform grid whose spacing increases with the argument. For large arguments, we introduce a normalized auxiliary function whose scaling and derivative properties allow it to be evaluated using the same Taylor procedure as the main-domain Boys functions. The main-domain and large-argument reference tables are constructed jointly, with polynomial degrees and grid parameters selected under accuracy and storage constraints. Low-part corrections to the reference values are included to improve the accuracy of the Taylor evaluation. The resulting method is implemented in the Fast and Accurate BOys (FABO) library and evaluated in QUICK and NWChem-Simint. FABO gives the smallest maximum and mean errors among the tested implementations for all three reported error measures, with the largest sampled error being approximately 1.067 units in the last place (ULPs). In application benchmarks, FABO reduces the Fock-build time relative to the original Boys evaluators in both applications and is competitive with the other tested implementations.

title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
summary: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.

title: HARI4D: Hand-Articulation Aware 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
summary: Reasoning about human-object interaction from RGB cameras is important for gaming, VR environments, and robot learning. Yet 4D reconstruction from a monocular RGB camera is challenging, especially when articulated hands are involved. Prior full-body works neglect hands during reconstruction, causing them to penetrate into, or float from the object. We present HARI4D, a hand-articulation-aware method for reconstructing spatially and temporally consistent 4D human-object interaction from monocular RGB video. We introduce a history-aware object tracker that provides robust and stable tracking. Based on these tracks, we improve the interaction configuration through coarse-to-fine reasoning that follows the order of object manipulation: ReachNet first brings the full body and arms to the object during contact, and TouchNet then finalizes hand articulation according to temporal context and local object geometry. On ARCTIC, unseen in training, our method reduces the object error by 56% and improves hand contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior art. Our method recovers accurate full body-object interaction with coherent hand articulations and applies to online videos. Our code and pretrained models will be released.

title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections
summary:
Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman--Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid.
  We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair.
  For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.

title: Whistler instability driven by electron trapping in magnetic dips
summary: Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, we show how free energy released by an ion-scale instability reaches electron scales through its effect on the electron distribution. An initial ion temperature anisotropy drives partly compressional ion cyclotron waves, which form magnetic dips. Electrons trapped in these dips develop an enhanced temperature anisotropy and butterfly-shaped distributions, similar to those observed by spacecraft in the Earth's magnetosheath. By tracking the energy transfer in velocity space, we show that the gradients created by trapping drive whistler waves through cyclotron resonance. The whistlers in turn scatter the electrons in pitch angle, flattening velocity-space gradients and heating the electrons along the magnetic field. As a result, the electron anisotropy drops to about half of the double-adiabatic prediction once the whistler power peaks. Our results show that it is the shape of the electron distribution in magnetic dips, rather than its temperature anisotropy alone, that drives the whistlers.

title: The Kelvin--Hicks Formula from the Energy--Casimir Principle
summary:
The classical Kelvin--Hicks formula expresses the propagation speed of a thin vortex ring in an incompressible ideal fluid in terms of its circulation, distance from the symmetry axis, and core radius. In this paper, we rigorously derive this formula from a variational principle based on Arnold's energy--Casimir method, without prescribing any of these geometric or physical quantities a priori. We introduce a scale-invariant variational principle involving the energy, impulse, and $L^p$ Casimir invariants. For $1 < p < \infty$, we construct orbitally stable energy-maximizing vortex rings and investigate how their geometry depends on the Casimir exponent $p$. For sufficiently large $p$, the vortex rings have cores homeomorphic to a ball and converge to Hill's spherical vortex as $p \to \infty$. In contrast, as $p\to1^+$, the energy-maximizing vortex rings concentrate onto a circular filament of radius $e^{1/3}$, uniquely selected by the variational principle. After suitable translations and rescalings, their vortex-core profiles converge to an optimizer of the logarithmic Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev inequality.
  Introducing an effective core radius $ε_p$ determined by the entropy of the vorticity distribution, we establish the Kelvin--Hicks formula \begin{align*} W_p = \frac{Γ_p}{4πR_p} \left(\log\frac{8R_p}{ε_p}-1+o(1)\right) \quad \textrm{as}\ p\to1^+, \end{align*} where $W_p$, $Γ_p$, and $R_p$ denote the propagation speed, circulation, and effective ring radius, respectively. In particular, the constant correction $-1$ is obtained for nonuniform vortex-core profiles without imposing any prescribed core structure.

title: SOARS: System One Assisted Reranking for Agentic Search
summary: Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve retrieval effectiveness but introduce substantial latency and cost when invoked throughout the search trajectory. We introduce SOARS, a training-free framework leveraging a System One model for fast, calibrated relevance estimation. At each search step, SOARS selects query-relevant passages from long documents and reranks candidates in a single call, jointly considering the original question and agent-generated sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on BrowseComp-Plus and WebShaper, SOARS consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, end-to-end latency, and inference cost. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GPT-5.4 Mini's accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while reducing search calls from 23 to 14, demonstrating the potential of System One reranking for more effective and efficient deep search.

title: From Fermions to Vortices: Microscopic Simulations of Phase Ordering in a d-Wave Superconductor
summary: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian remains a formidable challenge. Here we develop a microscopic framework for this problem using the recently introduced adiabatic variational principle (AVP) and demonstrate its application to a two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductor. The central construction maps evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with the associated Lagrange multipliers determining the thermodynamic driving forces. This enables dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining its microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Starting from disordered pairing configurations, we resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework. The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

title: IMPACT-Seg: Consistent Anatomical Segmentation and Representation Learning Across CT, CBCT, and MRI
summary:
Computed tomography (CT), cone-beam CT (CBCT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide complementary representations of the same underlying anatomy, yet substantial differences in image appearance challenge consistent segmentation and deformable registration in adaptive radiotherapy. We investigate whether dense anatomical segmentation supervision can promote cross-modality correspondence without explicit feature alignment. We introduce IMPACT-Seg, which segments 126 structures across CT, CBCT, and MRI using shared network parameters. A collection of 8,290 volumes was assembled from public cohorts through label harmonization, model-assisted pseudo-label completion, iterative refinement, and 2,864 physics-based CBCT simulations with voxel-aligned CT labels. Unpaired images were used to jointly train 2.5D and 3D residual-encoder networks.
  On 139 real CBCTs, IMPACT-Seg 3D achieved a mean Dice of 0.842 versus 0.671 for the strongest comparator. On 497 voxel-aligned CT-simulated-CBCT pairs, the CT-to-CBCT Dice decrease was 0.022 versus 0.153-0.178 for competing methods. On independent pancreatic radiotherapy CBCTs, gastrointestinal Dice was 0.735 versus 0.634 for TotalSegmentator. Prediction agreement reached 0.881 on registered CT-CBCT and 0.790 on CT-MRI pairs. Adding MRI training data reduced CT-MRI encoder feature retrieval error from 36.8 to 3.2 mm. Registration pipelines incorporating IMPACT-Seg features ranked first on two multimodal Learn2Reg benchmarks. The 3D model segmented a whole-body CT in 15 s.
  These findings show that dense anatomical segmentation supervision can support consistent anatomical representations across modalities, with applications to both segmentation and registration. Code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/HEMONCedric/IMPACTSeg.

title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
summary: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

title: Joint Detection of Constructive Speech, Hate Speech and Agreement in Online Conversations
summary: Online hate speech is an ever-growing issue with negative impacts on both groups and individuals, potentially causing users to withdraw from online conversations and debate. With some prominent social media platforms reducing their moderation efforts, constructive speech has emerged as an alternative strategy for countering hate. Automated detection of constructive and hateful speech can aid monitoring and improve understanding of their prevalence and online dynamics. In this work, we collect and annotate a large dataset of English and Danish social media comments for hateful tone, constructive tone, and agreement with parent comments. We fine-tune several multilingual LLMs to classify along these three dimensions and compare context-enriched and non-context-enriched model architectures. The E5-large LLM performs best on both the context-enriched (82% average F1) and non-context-enriched (81.6% average F1) classification tasks, demonstrating the potential of multilingual LLMs for scalable detection of hateful and constructive speech across languages.

title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
summary: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

title: Adaptive Electromagnetic Transient-level Digital Twins for Data Centers via In-Context Learning with LLMs
summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads has significantly increased data center (DC) power demand. Frequent operational and configurational changes, such as load surges caused by dynamic workload allocation, can induce electromagnetic transients (EMTs) whose accurate prediction is critical for reliable DC operation and maintenance. Although high-fidelity EMT solvers are widely adopted for transient analysis, their computational cost limits large-scale and multi-scenario studies. Digital twins address this computational bottleneck by emulating the behavior of a physical system and enabling fast prediction in place of expensive high-fidelity simulation. However,data-driven digital twins are non-adaptive and fail to generalize once the DC configuration changes. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an adaptive EMT-level digital twin for DCs based on in-context learning (ICL) with large language models (LLMs). We formulate the EMT prediction task as a system identification problem under parametric uncertainty and develop a GPT-2-based framework that adapts to unseen DC configurations at inference time from a small set of EMT trajectory samples, without model retraining. The proposed framework is validated on three representative EMT scenarios and benchmarked against three baseline non-adaptive twins. Results demonstrate superior prediction accuracy, improved adaptability to unseen operating conditions, and substantial computational speedups compared to high-fidelity EMT simulation.

title: Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) at the edge is increasingly desirable for privacy-sensitive applications and scenarios that require data to remain on local devices. However, edge environments are constrained by limited computational resources and exhibit substantial device heterogeneity, making efficient LLM serving challenging. These limitations become particularly pronounced under bursty demand, where congestion and queue buildup can significantly increase response latency. Replicating the model into multiple pipeline instances can improve serving capacity and reduce congestion. Yet, deciding how devices should be grouped into replicas, assigning replicas to prefill or decode functions, and partitioning model layers across heterogeneous devices jointly creates a large combinatorial optimization problem. We present Spade, a scalable and runtime-efficient placement planner for disaggregated LLM serving with pipeline replication across heterogeneous edge clusters. Spade introduces a dominance-based pruning technique that discards inferior replica candidates and recursively eliminates larger candidates that contain them, dramatically shrinking the search space. It further combines a water-filling approach for layer partitioning with a bounded multidimensional knapsack formulation that optimizes placement under a congestion-aware objective. On a synthetic fleet of 30 devices spanning five hardware classes, Spade finds the optimal placement in 441ms. In contrast, a genetic-search baseline augmented with dynamic-programming partitioning requires approximately two hours and still produces solutions with a 19.7% worse congestion objective. When evaluated on fleets containing ten device types, Spade's pruning strategy eliminates 99.6% of candidate placements while yielding the same surviving candidate set as exhaustive enumeration.

title: MemHand: Memory-Enhanced World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
summary: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. We will release our code and models at the project page: https://irmvlab.github.io/memhand.github.io

title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
summary: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.

title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
summary: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.

title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.

title: Weight Scale Rebalancing: Transferable Training Recipes for Transformers
summary: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $σ$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.

title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts
summary: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon\geq 0.5$) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon=0.5$, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. Code and data: https://github.com/Jamli58/fresh-keys-stale-secrets

title: Lensing ratios as a geometric probe of dark energy in the LSST and Simons Observatory era
summary: Ratios of galaxy-CMB and galaxy-galaxy lensing around the same foreground galaxies probe relative distances extending to recombination without a standard candle or ruler. For sufficiently narrow foreground redshift distributions, and with intrinsic alignments and lens magnification controlled, these lensing ratios (LRs) become geometrical. Here we characterize the geometrical limit and develop an end-to-end optimized framework for the probe with LSST Y10 and Simons Observatory uncertainties. In our forecast for LSST Y10, the individual ratios are measured to a median precision of 1.0%, with a total signal-to-noise ratio of 360. We then study the complementarity of LRs as an additional geometrical probe to constrain dark energy and curvature. We find that LRs improve the $w_0$-$w_a$ figure of merit of the combined CMB, Type Ia supernova, and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data by 15%, after marginalizing over systematic uncertainties. As an independent geometric probe, they also enable competitive leave-one-out tests, in which one of the probes is dropped, and we find they are most effective at replacing the BAO: adding LRs to CMB+supernova raises the figure of merit from 33% to 66% of that of the full CMB+supernova+BAO combination. We also find LRs are especially valuable in extended model spaces constrained with minimal assumptions: in a seven-bin reconstruction of the dark-energy density, they reduce per-bin uncertainties by up to 16% at $z>1$, and by up to 50% when freeing curvature and dropping the non-geometrical part of the CMB likelihood (i.e. keeping the acoustic angular scale part), where they are able to break the degeneracy between curvature and dark energy.

title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
summary: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.

title: MINDS: The mid-infrared spectrum of the disk, jets, and winds of DG Tau
summary: DG Tau is one of the best-studied young stellar objects in transition from a Class I protostar to a T Tauri star. It is no longer embedded in a dense molecular cloud, but still reveals features that are commonly seen in protostars at earlier evolutionary stages. DG Tau hosts a protoplanetary disk and two energetic jets that can be studied down to the immediate environment of the star and disk at optical, infrared, and X-ray wavelengths. We use the Medium Resolution Spectrometer of MIRI on the James Webb Space Telescope. DG Tau's mid-infrared spectrum consists of a very bright continuum with various silicate features, and lines of CO, H$_2$O, OH, H I, H$_2$, Ne$^{+}$, Ne$^{2+}$, Ar$^{+}$, Fe$^{+}$, and Ni$^{+}$. We find substantial grain growth to at least 2 $μ$m at an early evolutionary stage. Lines of H$_2$O and CO are formed at extremely high temperatures (600-2000 K). The ratio of warm to hot water is the lowest among previous observations of disks with JWST. This and a very strong continuum point toward the relevance of the strong accretion of DG Tau and consequently strong stellar UV irradiation. The pair of jets reveals a rich spectrum of emission lines from ions, in particular producing forbidden lines of [Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], and [Ni II]. The forward jet shows a collimated structure as found previously, while the hitherto poorly described, receding jet is more widely dispersed on scales of several arcsec, showing a layered structure with the fastest components being the most collimated. The ionization of the jet gas cannot be reconciled with high-energy radiation from the star itself. Instead, we propose a unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model in which the previously studied X-ray jet plasma continuously cools, recombining ions until, at temperatures around $10^4$ K and below, metals at low ionization stages emit the observed ion lines.

title: Speculative Decoding for Semantic-ID-Based Generative Recommendations
summary:
Generative recommender systems with Semantic IDs (SIDs) represent each item as a short sequence of $L$ discrete tokens and use a sequence model to predict the next item's tokens from a user's history. Industry-scale deployments typically use these models to retrieve multiple candidates per request with constrained beam search. However, this incurs a fixed cost of $L$ sequential model calls per request, and accuracy degrades as the SID generator becomes less sharp, without a guarantee on how close the output is to the exact top-$K$. Production systems therefore cannot detect degraded retrieval for individual requests.
  We propose SIDECAR, which uses approximate draft candidates and a tree-attention pass to score the entire draft in a single model call, memory permitting. This pass bounds the probability of every unexplored SID prefix and certifies the exact top-$K$ if the draft contains them. Otherwise, a branch-and-bound fallback expands only the parts of the trie that can still change the output, reaching certification within at most $L$ calls for any draft. Moreover, under a budget of $M$ tokens per call and $Y$ calls, which for $Y = L$ matches the resources of a beam search of width $M$, SIDECAR announces a factor $1 + δ$ within which its list will be exact at every rank. Depending on model sharpness, SIDECAR returns the exact top-$K$ using a fraction of beam search's calls or memory. Even when the budget is too small to recover the exact top-$K$, SIDECAR, unlike beam search, reports the announced factor, allowing the serving system to stop early once a quality target or latency limit is reached.

title: CORALIE Radial Velocity Search for Companions around Evolved Stars (CASCADES) VI. Revised masses and homogeneous estimation of the stellar parameters of 583 red giants
summary:
Giant-star radial-velocity surveys allow us to study how the exoplanet population varies with stellar mass and evolution. However, obtaining accurate estimates of stellar masses for such stars is challenging, as methods like isochrone fitting are prone to large errors due to the degeneracy associated with the closeness of isochrones.
  We provide a homogeneous re-derivation of the stellar parameters of the CASCADES giant-star survey. This includes parameters obtained from spectral energy distribution fitting, as well as an update of the stellar masses using asteroseismology.
  We use TESS light curves to measure the frequency of maximum oscillation power, $ν_{\rm max}$, for all the stars when applicable. We re-extract the stellar radii of the survey by fitting broadband photometry with ARIADNE, a spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting package, using priors from spectroscopy for the effective temperature, metallicity and $\log g$. By using scaling relations, we compute revised estimates of the stellar masses of targets with a $ν_{\rm max}$ measurement.
  We obtain new estimates of mass for 583 out of the 640 stars of the survey. These revised masses are typically 15 to 20% lower (median difference of $-0.35\,M_\odot$) than the ones obtained by isochrone fitting, in particular for low-metallicity stars for which this effect is stronger. These new masses impact the overall mass distribution of the sample, whose median decreases from $2.11\,M_\odot$ to $1.65\,M_\odot$.
  These revised masses provide the basis for future occurrence-rate analyses aiming to study the link between host-star mass and planet occurrence. They also highlight the uncertainties associated with the determination of masses for evolved stars.

title: PtychoFM: A Foundation Model for Ptychographic Imaging
summary: Ptychography provides high-resolution lensless imaging across X-ray, electron, and optical microscopy, but reconstructing images from diffraction measurements generally requires computationally intensity iterative phase retrieval. These methods often require experiment-specific analysis, limiting real-time feedback as data acquisition rates increase. Here, we demonstrate PtychoFM, a physics-aware foundation model for ptychographic imaging that combines large-scale pre-training with experiment-specific fine-tuning to reconstruct complex object images directly from individual diffraction patterns. Trained using a differentiable forward model without object-space labels, PtychoFM transfers from step-scan training data on one sample to fly-scan measurements of other samples with different feature sizes, morphologies, and refraction indices. At a synchrotron beamline, diffraction frames were streamed from the detector to a single GPU for inference at up to 200 frames per second and returned for real-time visualization. PtychoFM provides a practical route to rapid, transferable ptychographic reconstruction and live experimental feedback under nonideal conditions.

title: SAVERA: Bridging Frozen Vision and Language Models via Sparse Alignment and Visual Evidence Reuse
summary: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.

title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain
summary: Brain encoding models predict neural responses from audiovisual input, but typically overlook how ongoing brain activity shapes an individual's response. We introduce EEG-World, a recurrent world model that forecasts 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics from 6 seconds of preceding EEG and the subsequent audiovisual stimulus. Pretrained on continuous EEG, EEG-World learns shared neural dynamics and adapts to unseen individuals through lightweight subject-specific readouts. Using 2,584 hours of EEG from 78 participants, we show that nonlinear recurrent forecasting surpasses strong history-aware linear baselines at scale. EEG-World achieves a forecasting correlation of 0.261 versus 0.233 for the strongest history-and-video linear model, with a 3.3-second forecasting-horizon advantage. Its learned dynamics transfer to unseen participants, outperforming the linear baseline in 23 of 24 individuals after calibration. While ongoing EEG history accounts for most predictive performance, controlled stimulus analyses reveal an additional video-dependent component. This component also enables evaluation of visual representations, with V-JEPA 2 improving clip-locked prediction by 35% over combined CLIP and DINOv2 features. Our results demonstrate the value of transferable neural dynamics for individual EEG forecasting and highlight the importance of separating state-driven from stimulus-driven predictability.

title: PhysMend: Verification-Guided Program Refinement for Physics-Aware Video Generation
summary: Video generative models synthesize realistic scenes, yet their interactions often violate physics. A ball dropped onto sand should displace grains and settle into a crater, whereas a generated video may show it passing through the surface or leaving the sand flat. Post-hoc methods typically score generated videos with a vision-language model (VLM), but such scores offer limited guidance on which object or parameter to modify, and each correction costs another synthesis. Simulation-based pipelines instead run fixed stages before synthesis, so simulation errors reach the video. To address these limitations, we present PhysMend, a training-free framework for verification-guided program refinement. PhysMend describes the target event as an editable physical program of grounded objects, events, and required relations, paired with tunable execution parameters. Our key insight is to verify and repair the event on its simulated rollout and on the depth video that conditions the generator (depth control) rather than on generated videos, enabling quantitative violation measurement, targeted editing, and fast re-verification before synthesis. A hybrid verifier evaluates semantic event consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and visibility in the depth control. VLM judgments are confined to event semantics and cannot override failed physical measurements, which limits the impact of VLM hallucinations. Each failed check localizes the program fields eligible for repair, and its measured violation scales a bounded update of their parameters. Only accepted depth control reaches the generator, which runs once per input. Experiments on the commonly used benchmarks Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0 demonstrate substantial gains across different generator backbones; for example, PhysMend raises the overall Physics-IQ score of Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40.

title: Positive recurrence of weakly reversible stochastic reaction networks with mass-action kinetics
summary: We study finite stochastic reaction networks with mass-action kinetics. A network is weakly reversible if every reaction lies on a directed cycle of complexes. We prove that, for arbitrary positive rate constants, the Markov chain of every such network is non-explosive and positive recurrent on each communicating class. This settles the long-standing chemical recurrence conjecture. The proof is by construction of a Lyapunov function. For a fixed choice of weights on the species, the function is the exponential of a weighted count of the molecules, adjusted by a bounded quantity which is defined through the paths of reactions leading back to a reference population, and which accounts for the species that are absent or scarce. Before the adjusted count can decrease, several preparatory steps may be needed. We count faster and slower steps separately, giving priority to paths that require fewer slow steps. Weak reversibility controls how competing reactions can change these counts. Finitely many choices of weights are then combined, and a minimization over a scale parameter gives a single function on each communicating class.

title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?
summary: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.

title: Breaking the Joint Action Space Dependence in Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: We study the sample complexity of learning robust coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in finite-horizon, general-sum, distributionally robust Markov games with known rewards and a generative model of the nominal transitions. Each player evaluates a policy by its worst-case return over total-variation (TV) balls centered at the nominal transition distribution of every stage, state, and joint action; this is the standard $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set. Existing generative-model guarantees for this model scale with the number $\prod_iA_i$ of joint actions, where $A_i$ is the number of actions of player~$i$. Since this number grows exponentially with the number of players, these guarantees suffer from the curse of multiagency. We design an algorithm whose sample complexity depends on the action sets only through the largest individual action-set size $A_*:=\max_iA_i$. The algorithm uses $\widetilde O(SA_*H^5D^4/\varepsilon^4)$ transition samples and, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns a Markov policy that is an $\varepsilon$-robust CCE from every initial state. Here $S$ is the number of states, $H$ is the horizon, and $D:=\max_i\min\{H,1/ρ_i\}$, where $ρ_i$ is the TV radius of player~$i$. Two ingredients make this possible: a plug-in estimate of the robust backup whose mean error does not depend on the number of states, and a single batch of samples per round that serves as bandit feedback for all players at once. The result shows that the dependence on $\prod_iA_i$ can be avoided without modifying the $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set.

title: Interactive Neural Computers
summary: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor
summary: RL for LLMs often separates rollout generation from policy training. Although the two numerical engines share model parameters, they can induce different policies. This creates a challenge beyond correcting a known training-inference mismatch: during learner updates, the execution policy corresponding to the current parameters cannot be directly observed. We view this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor of its evolution. This perspective raises two fundamental questions: how can we estimate the execution policy's response to learner updates, and how much should we trust that estimate when optimizing the actual execution policy? We introduce Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (EPRO) to address these challenges. Starting from the observed rollout-time execution policy, we use training-policy changes to construct a differentiable predictor of the current execution policy, whose score yields Transported Score Centering (TSC). Our robust-improvement analysis reveals how prediction error limits the magnitude of reliably justified updates. For practical implementation, we introduce Policy Shift as an observable proxy for prediction risk and use Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates. Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
summary: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.

title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
summary: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis for scaling, compared to a single larger model. Finally, a third power law quantifies the loss of ensemble diversity as members share a larger fraction of training before branching, and therefore identifies a further limitation, beyond the capacity error, for LoRA ensembles and optimization-based or second-order methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution. At a high level, these findings suggest diverse ensembles can be a promising axis, both for scaling and uncertainty quantification at larger scales.

title: Supply Geometry, Learn Execution: Screw Attention for Zero-Shot Policy Transfer in Robot Manipulation
summary: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.

title: Is Prosody Encoded in the Neural Audio Codec Mimi?
